articleHeadline: Melioidosis Antibody Response Persists Years After Infection
articleSummary: Melioidosis antibody responses persist for years after infection, according to a Lancet Microbe retrospective cohort study from UC Davis and Mahidol University. In Thailand, researchers followed individuals after confirmed Burkholderia pseudomallei infection and found antibody levels against two diagnostic targets remained detectable long term, meaning positive antibody tests may reflect past exposure rather than current disease. Melioidosis, a serious infection transmitted through contact with soil and surface water contaminated with Burkholderia pseudomallei, causes fever, stomach pain, seizures and has a 10–50% fatality rate. Historically endemic in northern Australia and Southeast Asia (notably northeast Thailand), its geographic range appears expanding; in 2022 the CDC linked human cases in Mississippi to soil and water, signaling establishment in the continental US, with rising reports in South Asia and Africa. Climate change may broaden suitable environments, underscoring need for surveillance and clinician awareness.

articleSummary: Oropouche virus (Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense) surveillance from 1955 to early 2025 shows rapid spread beyond the Amazon with sustained transmission across South and Central America and imported infections in North America and Europe. Primary vector is Culicoides paraensis, with possible secondary vectors including Culex quinquefasciatus and several mosquitoes (Aedes serratus, Psorophora cingulata, Haemagogus tropicalis). After its 1955 isolation in Trinidad, the 1961 Belém urban outbreak (~11,000 cases) preceded Brazilian spread to Pará, Amapá, Amazonas, Maranhão and Goiás, with Brazil reporting about 500,000 infections (likely underestimated). International introductions began 1989 (Panama) and spread to Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Venezuela, Haiti, Colombia, French Guiana, and Cuba (2024). A late-2021 sublineage drives 2023–2025 activity; 2024 autochthonous Brazilian cases were 13,784 across 22 states, led by Espírito Santo and Rondônia. Outside Brazil: Peru 1,263; Cuba 626; Bolivia 356; plus imports to the United States and several European countries; WHO raised alert to high in August 2024. Severe disease includes confirmed vertical transmission with fetal deaths and congenital anomalies, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, and deaths in healthy adults. Deforestation, land-use change, urbanization, and climate warming fuel vector expansion.

articleHeadline: CSIR-CCMB team identifies potential new targets to fight Tuberculosis
articleSummary: Tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) remains a major public health challenge, with India accounting for about a quarter of global TB cases and roughly a third of drug-resistant infections per WHO Global TB Report 2025. articleHeadline: Study Analyzes Shifting Gonorrhea Trends and Regional Drivers Across
articleSummary: Gonorrhea incidence across mainland China shows significant spatiotemporal heterogeneity with a deepening north-south divide pre- and post-COVID-19, based on 31 provincial-level regions. The study tracks annual incidence with peaks in 2017, a pandemic-era drop in 2020, brief rebound in 2021, lowest in 2022, and a 2023 rebound. Global Moran's I increased from 0.2218 (2015) to 0.3338 (2023), indicating persistent regional clustering. Spatial nonstationarity is substantial: MGWR outperforms OLS (pre-pandemic adjusted R2 0.875 vs 0.252; post-pandemic 0.855 vs 0.301), revealing that GDP, health workforce, urbanization, and medical institutions influence local incidence differently than nationwide trends. Post-pandemic, health workforce effects homogenize, while population density effects localize. Policy implication: move to region-specific precision interventions, with active screening in southeastern hotspots and improved reporting in northwestern cold spots to offset underreporting.

articleSummary: Pertussis (Bordetella pertussis) in Kunming: retrospective study of 1,988 nucleic acid test-confirmed pediatric cases at Kunming Children's Hospital during 2024 shows a summer peak (July–August) and a bimodal age distribution with the highest incidence in infants <1 year and a secondary peak at age 7. articleHeadline: MSF calls for Ebola vaccine access to expand
articleSummary: MSF calls to expand ERVEBO Ebola vaccine access amid the Bundibugyo outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, urging WHO SAGE to lift current restrictions that confine ERVEBO to research programs. While not tailored to Bundibugyo virus, studies in animals and immune responses in vaccinated people suggest some protective effect, offering the best immediate way to reduce severe illness and deaths as Bundibugyo-specific vaccines are developed. No licensed vaccine exists for Bundibugyo; candidates are under development. MSF notes that from 2018–2024 over 365,000 people were vaccinated with ERVEBO in North Kivu and Ituri. The DRC government requested 500,000 doses in August via the International Coordinating Group, but only 70,000 were released. MSF urges Merck and partners to boost supply, and emphasizes vaccination must be paired with surveillance, testing, contact tracing, care, and community engagement to control the outbreak.

articleSummary: As of 10 November 2026, Thailand’s Department of Disease Control issues a winter health alert, urging vigilance for seven communicable diseases and two health threats. Four groups are highlighted: 1) Respiratory infections—influenza, pneumonia, RSV, and COVID-19; common symptoms include fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, headache, and body aches, with risk of breathing difficulty in young children and the elderly. Prevention stresses masks in crowded places, frequent handwashing, avoiding close contact with the ill, vaccination per guidance, and rest when sick. 2) Enteric/waterborne disease—acute diarrhea from contaminated food or water; symptoms include diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea and vomiting; prevention emphasizes cooking thoroughly, drinking clean water, using separate utensils, and handwashing before meals. 3) Vector-borne diseases—malaria (forest fringe areas) and scrub typhus (mite bites); symptoms include fever and myalgia; prevention includes covering skin and repellents, and noting travel history if fever after forest exposure. 4) Two winter health threats: cold-related illnesses/deaths and gas-powered water heater CO poisoning risks; precautions include warmth, nutrition, avoiding alcohol, ventilation, limiting baths to 10 minutes, and ventilating for 15–20 minutes after use. Monitoring is by 12 regional offices and the Urban Disease Control Institute with SRRT deployment; hotline 1422.
notes: 本記事はタイ疾病管理局による季節性の定例的な予防啓発発表であり、具体的な感染者数増加やアウトブレイクの報告はない。

articleHeadline: Development of real-time forecast modelling for lumpy skin disease outbreaks
articleSummary: Lumpy skin disease (LSD), a vector-borne, transboundary cattle disease spreading across East Asia and Europe, is the focus of a real-time forecasting model for early outbreak response. The model integrates intra- and inter-farm transmission, vector dynamics, and Approximate Bayesian Computation Sequential Monte Carlo (ABC-SMC) for iterative fitting. It compares two between-farm transmission schemes—force-based infectious pressure and stochastic infection probability—evaluated by continuous ranked probability scores. Validation used a simulated outbreak in Northern Australia and the 2024 LSD outbreak in Japan. The infection-probability approach achieved higher spatiotemporal accuracy than the infectious-pressure method, with the framework accurately capturing outbreak dynamics even when fit to only the first three weeks of data. The framework supports rapid decision-making across diverse national livestock systems and informs outbreak response strategies. Open access under CC BY 4.0.

articleSummary: Pulmonary tuberculosis admissions in Hainan, China, are linked to short-term exposure to PM2.5 and its chemical components. articleSummary: Twenty-six lymphatic filariasis risk prediction studies (2000–2025) were systematically reviewed and all were judged as high or unclear risk of bias, with external validation and calibration notably absent. Key pathogens linked to raw milk include Salmonella, Campylobacter, Listeria monocytogenes, and pathogenic Escherichia coli, causing severe abdominal cramps, vomiting, persistent diarrhea, dehydration, high fever, and potential kidney or neurological complications. Pasteurization—controlled heating—destroys harmful microorganisms while preserving nutrients; regulators such as Brazil’s Anvisa and the Ministry of Agriculture, and the U.S. CDC, recommend only pasteurized products for daily consumption. Vulnerable groups—young children, pregnant people, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals—face higher risks, underscoring the recommendation to choose certified pasteurized milk.

articleHeadline: Ghanaian Pediatric Study Finds Low Coinfection of Malaria and Enteric
articleSummary: In Northern Ghana's Kumbungu District, a hospital-based cross-sectional study at King's Medical Center (March–December 2024) assessed 239 children ≤12 years presenting with fever, diarrhea, or abdominal pain. Plasmodium falciparum malaria and enteric pathogens were detected individually, but concurrent infection occurred in only one child (0.4%). Malaria was confirmed via thick and thin blood films, with P. falciparum as the sole malaria species. Stool culture, following enrichment in selenite F broth and selective plating on MacConkey and XLD agar, plus Gram and biochemical confirmation, identified enteric pathogens. Fisher's exact tests showed no significant association between GI pathogens and malaria parasitemia. A significant link was found between household waste disposal methods and enteric pathogen positivity, underscoring sanitation as a driver of infections. Demographics: 63.6% male; median age 1.67 years (IQR 1.0–3.0); rural dwellers 72.8%. Sampling was consecutive; exclusions included prior antimicrobial/antimalarial therapy within two weeks.

articleSummary: Over 11,000 people have been confirmed infected with Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), with 5,387 deaths, according to authorities as of 11 November 2026. A total of 11,042 cases have been registered since the outbreak began in May. This outbreak ranks as the second-largest and second-deadliest on record, surpassed only by West Africa’s 2014–2016 epidemic, which infected over 28,600 and killed about 11,000. The transmission is driven by the Bundibugyo ebolavirus variant, for which there are no approved vaccines or treatments. Delayed detection, armed conflict, and a strained health system have facilitated faster spread than in prior outbreaks. Ebola has now been detected across East, Central, and West Africa, marking the widest geographic spread recorded on the African continent.
